Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: 'Arguments' is a weak fit as a primary trigger for PTSD related to a life-threatening illness when the rest of the profile is dominated by somatic danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and self-appraisals about coping. It is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-centered threat pattern and lacks support from memory/appraisal content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict eating to feel in control' is not well integrated with the rest of the formulation. The active edges emphasize threat and negative appraisals leading to maladaptive strategies, but the other selected strategies are cognitive/self-punitive and illness-related themes are otherwise absent from eating control. In this profile it looks like a strategy addressing a different problem domain unless additional body/illness-control content were present.

vignette:
Leilani, a 46-year-old singer and musician from a Pacific Islander community, nearly died two years ago from a sudden, severe case of pneumonia that landed her in the ICU on a ventilator. The memory of gasping for air, the antiseptic burn of the hospital corridors, and the cold pressure of the oxygen mask are still vivid - but it is not the event itself that haunts her. It is what her body does now. A slight tightness in her chest during a rehearsal makes her freeze; the scent of bleach in a public restroom sends her heart racing; a routine blood pressure check at the pharmacy triggers a wave of dread that leaves her shaking. She has come to believe that if she does not stay hypervigilant, her body might betray her again.

Leilani wakes several times each night, sitting up abruptly to check whether her breathing is steady, even before her conscious mind has caught up with the panic. "My body reacts before I have time to think," she says, and this frightens her most of all. She now feels safe only in a handful of places: her own home, a small practice room at the community center, and her husband's car. Anywhere outside that circle is potential danger. Because her heightened threat system is constantly scanning for signs of physical vulnerability, she notices every slight shortness of breath - a sensation most people would ignore becomes, for her, a signal of impending collapse. The threat also feeds her growing self-doubt. "I can't trust that I will do the right thing anymore," she confesses. She sees herself as fundamentally inadequate - a lousy coper who cannot handle what others manage without effort. Every time her body alarms before her mind, she takes it as proof that she is weak.

These negative appraisals drive her maladaptive strategies. Believing she is a bad coper, Leilani replays the illness over and over: "If only I had gone to the doctor the first day I coughed, life would be different." She tells herself she deserves to suffer for not taking better care of her health - a form of punishment thinking that keeps her trapped in shame. And because she is convinced she cannot cope with medical settings, she now avoids them entirely. She canceled her annual physical, refused a follow-up pulmonary test, and asks her husband to pick up her prescriptions so she does not have to step into the clinic. The threat itself also directly reinforces her avoidance: the hyperarousal that jolts her awake at night makes even the thought of a hospital feel unbearable, so she stays away. And her limited safe zone has narrowed her daily life to the point where she no longer agrees to perform at venues with strong cleaning smells or crowded backstage areas.

Leilani is a professional musician, but her world has shrunk. She used to sing at community festivals and wedding receptions; now she only practices in her basement, where she controls the air and the smells. Her husband has grown worried - she has lost income, and she has stopped seeing friends who might want to meet at a café that smells of hand sanitizer. What finally brought her to therapy was a rehearsal last month: a short duet made her feel breathless, she became convinced she was suffocating, and she fled the stage. "I couldn't even finish a single song," she whispered. She is terrified that her career is over, and she is equally afraid that seeking help will confirm once and for all that she is a bad coper. But even more than that, she hopes to one day walk into a doctor's office without her body screaming danger, and to sing again without the fear that each breath might be her last.
